title: Putting together and taking away

summary.text: There were 7 beans. A cup hides some of them, and you can still tell how many are under it. How? You will put heaps of beans together and take beans away, to find out what each does to a number. You will test whether 5 and 3 make the same as 3 and 5, and whether taking away works the same way. You will learn to write it as a sum, with the signs +, − and =. And you will find that one move can be taking away for you and adding for someone else.
summary.art: A girl and her mother on a kitchen floor with two small steel plates of rajma beans and one big plate between them, the girl tipping one small plate onto the big one.

intro.hook: There were 7 beans. Now you can see only 4. How many are hiding under the cup?
intro.text: 3 beans are under the cup. Here is one way to know. Start at 4 and count on until you reach 7: 5, 6, 7. That is 3 more. Nobody had to lift the cup. When things are put together or taken away, you can work out the new number without seeing them all. In this lesson you will find out how, with beans.
intro.art: An upturned steel tumbler on a floor with four beans beside it, and a child bending down to peek under its rim.

outcomes: I can put two groups together and say how many there are in all, up to 20.
I can take some away from a group and say how many are left.
I can read and write a sum with the signs +, − and =.
I can count on to add and count back to take away, on a number line.
I can show that adding works in either order, and that taking away does not.
I can say what happens when I add zero, take away zero, or take away everything.
I can say that one move can be taking away for one person and adding for another.
I can give a total a name that fits both groups: 3 idlis and 2 vadas are 5 things to eat.

terms.meaning: To put two groups together and find how many there are in all.
terms.example: 4 spoons and 2 more spoons. You add them and get 6 spoons.

explanations.context: This card says what adding is, with a worked example. You did it in the Two Plates Test when you tipped two heaps of beans together.
explanations.definition: To add is to put two groups together and find how many there are in all.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. There are 5 idlis on the plate. Paati puts 3 more on it. To find how many there are now, you can count them all: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. Or you can count on. You know there are 5, so start at 5 and say 6, 7, 8. Either way there are 8 idlis. We say '5 and 3 make 8', or '5 plus 3 equals 8'. The answer is called the total. Now you try: put 4 spoons and 2 spoons together.
examples: 4 red bangles and 2 green bangles make 6 bangles.
7 children are in the auto. 1 more gets in. Now there are 8.
10 beans in a full ten-frame and 4 beans beside it make 14 beans.
explanations.art: A steel plate with five idlis and a grandmother's hand adding three more from a steamer plate.

explanations.context: This card says what taking away is, with a worked example. You did it in the Two Plates Test when you took 3 beans from 8.
explanations.definition: To subtract is to take some away from a group and find how many are left.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. There are 8 bananas in the bunch. The family eats 3. To find how many are left, take 3 away and count the rest: 5. Or count back three from 8: 7, 6, 5. We say '8 take away 3 leaves 5', or '8 minus 3 equals 5'. When you take some away, the number left is smaller than the number you started with. It stays the same only when you take away nothing. Now you try: take 2 spoons away from 6 spoons.
examples: 9 dosas were made. 4 were eaten. 5 dosas are left.
6 crows sat on the wire. 2 flew off. 4 crows are still there.
12 eggs were in the tray. Amma used 2 for the curry. 10 eggs are left.
explanations.art: A bunch of eight bananas on a table with three peeled skins beside it and five bananas still on the bunch.

explanations.concept: Writing it down: the signs +, − and =
explanations.context: This card shows how to write adding and taking away with signs, so that anyone can read it.
explanations.definition: A sum is a short way to write adding or taking away. It uses numbers and the signs +, − and =.
explanations.description: The sign + is read 'plus'. It means put together. The sign − is read 'minus'. It means take away. The sign = is read 'equals'. It means that both sides are the same amount. So '5 and 3 make 8' is written 5 + 3 = 8. And '8 take away 3 leaves 5' is written 8 − 3 = 5. You can also write a sum going down, one number under the other, with a line above the answer. Both ways say the same thing. People chose these signs, and they could have chosen others. An old Indian maths book, the Bakhshali manuscript, was written more than a thousand years ago. In it, a small cross after a number meant 'take this away'.
examples: 2 + 2 = 4 is read 'two plus two equals four'.
10 − 1 = 9 is read 'ten minus one equals nine'.
5 = 5 is true. 5 = 6 is not true, because the two sides are not the same amount.
explanations.art: A slate showing 5 + 3 = 8 written across, and beside it the same sum written going down with a line above the 8.

explanations.concept: Adding works in either order. Taking away does not.
explanations.context: In the Two Plates Test you tipped two heaps together in both orders, and you tried to take away in both orders. This card says what you found.
explanations.definition: When you add two numbers, you can swap them and the total stays the same. When you take away, you cannot swap them.
explanations.description: You tipped 5 beans and then 3 beans. You got 8. Then you tipped 3 beans and then 5 beans. You got 8 again. They are the same beans, so the total cannot change. This is true for every pair of numbers: 9 + 7 and 7 + 9 are both 16. It is also a useful trick. To work out 2 + 9, start with the bigger number, 9, and count on only two: 10, 11. Taking away is different. 8 − 3 is 5. But with beans you cannot do 3 − 8, because after you take 3 the plate is empty.
examples: 1 + 8 is quicker as 8 + 1. Start at 8 and count on one: 9.
7 − 2 = 5. But 2 − 7 cannot be done with 2 beans.
explanations.art: Two big plates side by side, each holding the same eight beans, one labelled '5 then 3' and the other '3 then 5'.

chart.title: Count each row. Both rows are 8.

explanations.concept: Counting on and counting back on a number line
explanations.context: This card shows how to add and take away by hopping along a number line. You use it in the game Heads Add, Tails Take Away.
explanations.definition: A number line is a line of numbers in counting order. To add, you hop forward. To take away, you hop back.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example of adding. For 9 + 4, put your finger on 9. Hop forward four times: 10, 11, 12, 13. You land on 13, so 9 + 4 = 13. Here is a worked example of taking away. For 13 − 4, put your finger on 13. Hop back four times: 12, 11, 10, 9. You land on 9, so 13 − 4 = 9. Be careful about one thing. The number you start on is not a hop. Your first hop lands on the next number.
examples: 6 + 3: start on 6 and hop 7, 8, 9. The answer is 9.
15 − 2: start on 15 and hop back 14, 13. The answer is 13.
17 + 3: start on 17 and hop 18, 19, 20. The answer is 20.
explanations.art: A number line from 0 to 20 with a finger on 9 and four curved hops forward landing on 13.

chart.title: Start on 9. Hop forward 4. Where do you land?

explanations.concept: Sums up to 20 with a ten-frame
explanations.context: This card shows how to add and take away with beans when the numbers go past ten.
explanations.definition: A ten-frame is a box with ten spaces, in two rows of five. A full frame is ten. So you can see a number from 11 to 20 as ten and some more.
explanations.description: Here is a worked example. For 8 + 5, put 8 beans in a ten-frame. Hold 5 more beans in your hand. Two spaces in the frame are empty, so 2 of your beans fill them. Now the frame is full, and that is 10. You still have 3 beans, and they go beside the frame. Ten and three is 13. So 8 + 5 = 13. To take away, lift beans off. For 13 − 5, lift the 3 loose beans first, and then 2 more from the frame. 8 beans are left.
examples: 10 + 6 = 16: a full frame and 6 more.
9 + 2: one bean fills the frame and the other bean stays outside. That is 11.
14 − 4 = 10: lift the 4 loose beans, and the full frame is left.
explanations.art: A ten-frame drawn on paper with eight beans in it and a child's hand holding five more beans above the two empty spaces.

chart.title: There is a gap after every 5. Two fives make ten.

explanations.concept: Adding nothing, taking away nothing, taking away everything
explanations.context: This card is about sums with zero in them.
explanations.definition: Zero means none. Adding zero or taking away zero leaves a number as it was. Taking away all of a number leaves zero.
explanations.description: Put 6 beans on a plate. Add no beans. There are still 6, so 6 + 0 = 6. Take no beans away. There are still 6, so 6 − 0 = 6. Now take all 6 away. The plate is empty, so 6 − 6 = 0. An Indian mathematician named Brahmagupta wrote these rules down in the year 628, in a book in Sanskrit. They are the oldest rules we know of for adding and taking away with zero.
examples: 4 + 0 = 4. Nothing was added.
9 − 0 = 9. Nothing was taken away.
5 − 5 = 0. Five laddus were on the plate, five were eaten, and none are left.
explanations.art: Three steel plates in a row: six beans, six beans with an empty hand above, and an empty plate.

explanations.concept: Taking away here is adding there
explanations.context: In the Two Plates Test you gave 2 of your beans to your grown-up. This card says what happened to the numbers.
explanations.definition: When things move from one place to another, one place has fewer and the other has more. The number in both places together does not change.
explanations.description: You had 5 beans and your grown-up had 5. You gave 2. Your plate went from 5 down to 3. That is 5 − 2 = 3. Their plate went from 5 up to 7. That is 5 + 2 = 7. It was one move. For you it was taking away. For them it was adding. Together you still had 10 beans. The same thing happens when Amma takes 2 idlis from the big plate and puts them on yours. The big plate has 2 fewer, and your plate has 2 more.
examples: 4 people get off the bus at a stop. The bus has 4 fewer people and the stop has 4 more.
You pour water from a jug into a tumbler. The jug has less and the tumbler has more.
In the game Pallanguzhi, seeds move from cup to cup. One cup has fewer and the next cups have more.
explanations.art: Two small plates of beans with an arrow showing two beans moving from the child's plate to the mother's plate.

explanations.concept: Before you add: one name for both heaps
explanations.context: This card is about a choice people make before they add. You try it in the activity Five What?
explanations.definition: You can add two groups when you count both as the same kind of thing. The total gets a name that fits both groups.
explanations.description: Put 3 idlis and 2 vadas on a plate. Are there 5? It depends on what you are counting. There are not 5 idlis, and there are not 5 vadas. But there are 5 things to eat. To add the two groups, you first choose a name that fits both. In the same way, 4 tomatoes and 3 onions make 7 vegetables. And 2 girls and 3 boys make 5 children. The sum 3 + 2 = 5 is always right. What people choose is which things to count under one name.
examples: 5 chappals and 2 shoes are 7 pieces of footwear.
2 cats and 2 crows are 4 animals. They are not 4 cats.
If someone asks 'How many idlis?', the answer is still 3. The vadas are not counted.
explanations.art: A banana leaf with three idlis and two vadas, and three labels pointing at it: '3 idlis', '2 vadas', '5 things to eat'.

explanations.concept: When 1 and 1 do not make 2: drops and dough
explanations.context: This card is about things that join when you put them together. You try it in the activity When 1 and 1 Make 1.
explanations.definition: Adding numbers fits things that stay separate when you put them together. Some things do not stay separate. They join into one.
explanations.description: Put one drop of water on a dry steel plate. Put another drop beside it. Push them together with your finger. Now there is one drop, not two. The same happens when two balls of chapati dough are pressed together: one ball. Is 1 + 1 = 2 wrong? No. The big drop has all the water of both small drops. If you measure the water in spoonfuls, or weigh the dough, the adding works. It does not work for counting drops or balls, because they did not stay separate. So before you add, check what you are counting.
examples: 2 heaps of rice pushed together make 1 heap. But 2 cups of rice and 1 cup of rice still make 3 cups of rice.
2 beans stay 2 beans, however close you push them.
1 rope tied to 1 rope makes 1 longer rope.
explanations.art: A steel plate with two water drops and a finger pushing them, and beside it the same plate with one bigger drop.

explanations.concept: Adding and taking away are happening all around you
explanations.context: This card looks for adding and taking away in your own body, in the sky and in the kitchen.
explanations.definition: Many changes around you are one of two kinds. Something joins, or something leaves.
explanations.description: Look in your own mouth. A small child has 20 milk teeth, 10 on top and 10 below. From about the age of six they fall out, a few each year, and bigger teeth grow in their place. Each tooth that falls is 'take away one'. Look at the Moon. For about two weeks the bright part grows a little every night, until the full Moon. Then for about two weeks it shrinks a little every night, until the new Moon. The Indian calendar cuts the growing time into 15 steps and the shrinking time into 15 steps. Each step is called a tithi. Look at the bananas on the table. Every day there are fewer, until someone buys more.
examples: A hen lays an egg. Now the nest has one more.
A neem tree drops old leaves and grows new ones.
People get on and off a bus at every stop.
explanations.art: A smiling six-year-old girl showing a gap where a front milk tooth has fallen out, with a thin crescent Moon in the window behind her.

explanations.concept: Chicks, bees and babies follow adding and taking away too
explanations.context: This card is about other living beings, and human babies, keeping track of things added and taken away. It says what scientists found and what they still argue about.
explanations.description: Humans are not the only animals who can follow adding and taking away. In 2009 Rosa Rugani and other scientists in Italy tested chicks who were about three days old. Each chick had grown up with five small yellow balls and liked to stay near them. While the chick watched, the scientists hid some balls behind one screen and some behind another. Then they moved balls from one screen to the other, one at a time. The chick could not see behind the screens. When the chick was let go, about three times in four they walked to the screen with more balls behind it. In 2019 Scarlett Howard and other scientists in Australia trained 14 honeybees. A blue picture meant 'choose the picture with one more shape'. A yellow picture meant 'choose the one with one fewer'. The bees were right about two times in three. And in 1992 Karen Wynn tested human babies who were five months old. The babies looked for longer when one doll and one more doll seemed to make only one doll.
examples: A chick sees 4 balls go behind one screen and 1 behind the other. Then 2 are moved across. Now it is 2 and 3, and the chick walks to the 3.
A bee sees 2 blue shapes, flies on, and picks the picture with 3 shapes.
A baby sees one doll go behind a screen, and then one more. The screen drops and only one doll is there. The baby stares for longer.

perspectives.who: Scientists who say this is adding and taking away
perspectives.explanation: The chicks could not see the balls at the end. To choose right, they had to keep track of each ball that was added and each ball that was taken away. That is what adding and taking away are.

The numbers were small, five or fewer. The chicks and the babies may be keeping track of each thing one by one, in a way that is not like our numbers. And the babies may have been looking at how much doll they could see, not how many dolls. So it is safer to say that these beings keep track of more and fewer in their own way.

explanations.art: A small yellow chick in a white arena looking at two upright screens, with a yellow ball being moved on a thread from one screen to the other.

chart.title: Then 2 balls move from A to B. Which screen hides more now?

explanations.concept: Stretch: can you take away more than you have?
explanations.context: This card goes further than Class 1. It is for a child who asks what happens when you try to take 8 from 5.
explanations.definition: A debt is what you owe. People use numbers below zero to write a debt.
explanations.description: With beans you cannot take 8 away from 5. After 5 the plate is empty. But think about money. You have 5 rupees and you must pay 8. You pay your 5, and you still owe 3. People found ways to write 'owe 3'. In China, more than 1,700 years ago, the mathematician Liu Hui wrote about counting sticks in two colours. Red sticks stood for what you have, and black sticks for what you owe. In India, Brahmagupta wrote rules for 'fortunes' and 'debts' in the year 628. Today we write a debt of 3 as −3, and we read it 'minus three'. On a number line it sits three hops to the left of zero.
examples: A lift goes down from floor 0 to the basement. Some lifts show the basement as −1.
A cold night is 2 degrees. It gets 5 degrees colder. Now it is 3 degrees below zero.
Meena has 4 seeds and must give 6. She gives 4 and owes 2.
explanations.art: A number line running from −5 to 5 with zero in the middle, red sticks laid above the numbers to the right and black sticks above the numbers to the left.

chart.title: A number line that goes below zero. The pointer is on −3.

agreed.text: When you add two heaps, you can start with either heap. The total is the same.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test it with beans. Tip 5 and then 3, and count. Tip 3 and then 5, and count. It is 8 both times, because they are the same beans. You tested this in the Two Plates Test.

agreed.text: If you take some beans away from a heap, fewer beans are left. Never more.
agreed.evidence: Take 1, 2 or 3 beans from a heap of 8 and count what is left each time: 7, 6, 5. The number only goes down. It stays the same only if you take none.

agreed.text: Adding nothing, or taking away nothing, leaves a number just as it was.
agreed.evidence: 6 beans with no beans added are still 6 beans. Brahmagupta wrote this rule in India in the year 628.

agreed.text: When beans only move from one plate to another, the number on both plates together does not change.
agreed.evidence: Give 2 of your 5 beans to someone who has 5. You have 3 and they have 7. Count both plates together: still 10.

agreed.text: A baby who is five months old already seems to expect that one doll and one more doll make two dolls.
agreed.evidence: In 1992 Karen Wynn showed babies one doll going behind a screen, and then one more. When the screen dropped and only one doll was there, the babies looked for longer, as people do when something is not what they expected. Other scientists have repeated the test. They still argue about what the babies are thinking.

challenging.claim: Adding always makes more, and taking away always makes less.
challenging.context: This card is about a rule that is nearly always true, and the times when it is not.
challenging.for: With beans it is true whenever you add or take away at least one bean. 5 + 1 is more than 5, and 5 − 1 is less than 5.
challenging.against: Add zero and the number stays the same: 5 + 0 = 5. Later, with numbers below zero, adding a debt makes less. So the rule holds only when you add or take away one or more real things.

challenging.claim: One and one always make two.
challenging.context: This card is about whether 1 + 1 = 2 fits everything you can put together.
challenging.for: For numbers this is always true: 1 + 1 = 2. One bean and one bean are two beans, for everyone, everywhere.
challenging.against: One drop of water pushed into another drop makes one drop. One ball of dough pressed into another makes one ball. The sum is not wrong. It just does not fit things that join. It fits things that stay separate.

challenging.claim: You can never take a bigger number from a smaller one.
challenging.who: Many mathematicians in Europe, for hundreds of years
challenging.context: This card is about an old argument: what is 3 take away 8?
challenging.for: With beans it is true. Nobody can take 8 beans from a plate of 3.
challenging.against: With money you can owe. Brahmagupta in India wrote rules for debts in the year 628, and mathematicians in China used black counting sticks for debts even earlier. Today everyone uses numbers below zero, for money owed and for very cold days.

challenging.claim: Only humans can add and take away.
challenging.context: This card is about whether other living beings do what we call adding and taking away.
challenging.for: Only humans write sums, use signs such as + and −, and add big numbers.
challenging.against: In tests, chicks three days old, honeybees, some fish and human babies have all kept track of small numbers of things being added and taken away. Nobody taught the chicks.

big_questions.q: You give your sister 2 of your beans. Is that adding or taking away?
5 + 3 and 3 + 5 are both 8. Why can it never come out different?
big_questions.hint: Think about the beans. Did any bean come or go?

big_questions.q: Can you add 3 idlis and 2 vadas? If the answer is 5, it is 5 of what?
big_questions.hint: Look for one name that fits both.

big_questions.q: When you eat an idli, it is taken away from the plate. Where is it added?
Is anything in the world truly gone when it is taken away?
big_questions.hint: Think of a puddle drying, a candle burning and a balloon popping.

big_questions.q: A chick can follow balls being added and taken away. Is the chick doing maths?
big_questions.hint: What would the chick have to do for you to say yes?

story.title: Don't Lift the Lid
story.note: Kayal, Murugan, Paati and the customers are made up. The Meenakshi temple, Alagar Kovil and the Government Rajaji Hospital are real places in and near Madurai.
text: Kayal's grandmother sold idlis from a cart near the East Tower of the Meenakshi temple in Madurai. The idlis sat in a big steel box with a tight lid, wrapped in a white cloth to keep the steam in.
Kayal was seven. In the Pongal holidays she came every morning to help. Her cousin Murugan, who was ten, came too. He carried the chutney buckets and told Kayal what to do.

That morning, before the sun was up, a teacher on a scooter stopped at the cart. "Paati, I am taking my class to Alagar Kovil today," she said. "I need ten idlis for the children at seven o'clock. Will you keep ten for me?"
"Ten idlis at seven," said Paati. "They will be here."
When the teacher had gone, Paati lifted the lid. Steam rushed out. Kayal counted with her, pointing at each idli. "Twenty," she said.

Paati shut the lid and tucked the cloth around it. "Now listen, both of you. I must go home and grind the next batter. Every time this lid is lifted, the steam gets out and the idlis go hard and cold. So do not lift it to look. Lift it only to serve. Five more idlis are in the steamer. Thangam akka at the next cart will tell you when they are done."
"If we cannot look, how will we know there are ten left for the teacher?" asked Murugan.
"You will find a way," said Paati, and she went.

An auto driver came first. "Three idlis, thangachi." Murugan lifted the lid just enough, took out three and shut it again. Kayal held up her fingers. "Twenty," she whispered. "Nineteen, eighteen, seventeen. Seventeen."
"What are you muttering?" said Murugan.
"Nothing," said Kayal.
A flower seller bought two. "Sixteen, fifteen," said Kayal under her breath. "Fifteen."
A nurse on her way to the Government Rajaji Hospital bought four. Kayal folded down four fingers, one for each number. "Fourteen, thirteen, twelve, eleven. Eleven."

Then Thangam akka called from the next cart. "Your idlis are done!" Murugan carried the hot plate over and slid five new idlis into the box. This time Kayal counted upward. "Eleven. Twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen. Sixteen."
The street was filling up. A man in a white veshti got off a bus with a big tiffin carrier. "Six idlis," he said. "Quickly, my bus is leaving."
Murugan did not move. "We cannot," he said. "The teacher needs ten. I saw the box when I put the new ones in. It looked less than half full. If we sell six, there will not be enough."
"There will be enough," said Kayal.
"You have not even looked!"

"I do not need to look. There were twenty. Three went, then two, then four. That left eleven. Five came. That made sixteen." She looked at her fingers. "Sixteen take away six. Fifteen, fourteen, thirteen, twelve, eleven, ten. Ten will be left. Exactly ten."
"Fingers are not idlis," said Murugan. "Let me lift the lid and count properly."
"Paati said not to. And the man's bus is leaving."

Murugan looked at the bus. He looked at the box. He looked at his small cousin, who was holding up ten fingers and not blinking. He lifted the lid a crack, took out six idlis without looking at the rest, and shut it. The man paid and ran.
After that nobody came. Murugan kept glancing at the box. "If there are only eight in there," he said, "you are the one who tells the teacher."
"There are ten," said Kayal. But her stomach felt tight, and she went over the numbers again in her head. Twenty. Seventeen. Fifteen. Eleven. Sixteen. Ten.
At seven o'clock the scooter came round the corner. Paati was walking behind it with the new batter on her hip.
"My ten idlis?" said the teacher.
Paati looked at the two children. Murugan looked at Kayal. Kayal nodded.

Paati lifted the lid. Steam rushed out, thick and white. She took the idlis out one at a time and laid them on a banana leaf, and Murugan counted every one aloud. "One. Two. Three." His voice got slower. "Eight. Nine. Ten."
The box was empty. The idlis were soft and hot.
Paati wrapped the leaf and handed it over. Then she turned to the children. "Who lifted the lid to count?"
"Nobody," said Murugan. He pointed his chin at Kayal. "She counted them without seeing them. Every time some went out, and when the new ones came in."
Paati laughed. "Then from tomorrow," she said, "Kayal keeps the count, and you carry the chutney."
Murugan picked up the bucket. "Kayal," he said after a while. "Show me how you did it with your fingers."
story.epiphany: For the parent: adding and taking away let you keep track of a number you cannot see. Kayal never looked in the box. She changed her number each time idlis went out or came in, and her number stayed true.
ask: Kayal never looked inside the box. How did she know how many idlis were in it?
When the five new idlis went in, Kayal counted upward. Why did she change direction?
Murugan said, 'Fingers are not idlis.' He was right. So why did the fingers still work?
What at home could you keep count of without looking?
