experiments.title: The Two Plates Test: does it matter which heap goes first?
experiments.context: In this test you put two heaps of beans together, first one way round and then the other. Then you try the same with taking away. Last, you give some of your beans to your grown-up. Before each step you guess what the count will be. You will find out when the order matters, and whether beans that are given away are lost.
experiments.question: When we put two heaps together, does it matter which heap goes first? Does the order matter when we take away? And when beans move from one plate to another, is any bean lost?
experiments.predict: Before each step, guess what the count will be: more, fewer or the same as before? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same beans each time. Nobody adds a bean or takes one away unless the step says so. We count by sliding each bean, so that no bean is counted twice. We try more than one pair of heaps, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: dried beans such as rajma or chana, or tamarind seeds or buttons, all about the same size
paper and a pencil, for the table

experiments.safety: Keep beans and seeds away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Put two heaps of beans together in both orders. Try to take away in both orders. Then give beans from one plate to another and count both plates.

experiments.record: A grown-up draws the table. For each step, write the guess and then the count. At the end the child says what they found, and the grown-up writes it under the table.

example_chart.title: What a finished table can look like (your guesses will be your own)

setup.art: Two small steel plates, one with five rajma beans and one with three, beside a big empty plate on a kitchen floor.
setup.caption: 1. Put 5 beans on one small plate and 3 on the other.

setup.art: A child tipping the plate of five beans onto the big plate, with the plate of three waiting beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Tip both onto the big plate and count. Then do it in the other order.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up sitting face to face, each with a small plate of five beans, the child's hand passing two beans across.
setup.caption: 3. Last, give 2 of your beans across and count both plates.

flow.do: 1. Draw the table on paper. 2. Your child puts 5 beans on one small plate and 3 on the other. 3. Your child tips the 5 onto the big plate, and then the 3. 4. Your child counts the big plate. Write '5 and 3 make 8'.
flow.say: Here are 5 beans, and here are 3 beans. Tip them together on the big plate. How many are there now?
flow.kid: Put 5 beans on one plate and 3 on the other. Tip them onto the big plate. Count them all.

ask.q: Did you count them all from 1, or did you start from 5?
good: I counted them all: 1, 2, 3, up to 8.
I started at 5 and said 6, 7, 8.

flow.parent: Both ways are right. Counting on from 5 is quicker, and most children find it by themselves after a few goes. Do not teach it yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Two Plates Test. You put a heap of 5 beans and a heap of 3 beans together, and count.

flow.do: 1. Put 5 beans and 3 beans back on the small plates. 2. Say that this time the 3 will go first. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write the guess. 4. Your child tips the 3, then the 5, and counts.
flow.say: Last time the 5 went first. This time the 3 goes first. Will we get more, fewer or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Now the 3 beans go first, then the 5. Guess: more, fewer or the same? Then count.

good: It is the same beans, so it will be the same.
The big heap goes last, so maybe more.
I am not sure. Let us count.

flow.parent: Many six-year-olds are not sure. Accept any guess that comes with a reason. Let the count answer: it is 8 again.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the Two Plates Test. The same two heaps are put together in the other order, and you guess before you count.

flow.do: 1. Your child picks two new numbers of beans, each from 2 to 9. 2. Write a guess: will both orders give the same number? 3. Your child tips them together one way and counts. 4. Then the other way. Write both counts.
flow.say: Now you choose the two heaps. Will it be the same both ways again? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Pick two new heaps. Put them together one way and count. Then try the other way.

ask.q: Could there be a pair of heaps where the order changes the answer?
good: No. It is always the same beans.
I tried, and I could not find one.

flow.parent: With 9 and 7 the total is 16. If a count goes wrong past ten, slide the beans across one by one while counting. Try a third pair if your child wants to be sure.
flow.context: This is step 3 of the Two Plates Test. You choose two new heaps of beans and put them together in both orders.

chart.title: An example. Your two heaps will be your own.

flow.do: 1. Put 8 beans on the big plate. 2. Ask how many will be left if 3 are taken away. Write the guess. 3. Your child takes 3 away and counts what is left. 4. Now put only 3 beans on the plate. Ask your child to take 8 away.
flow.say: There are 8 beans. Take 3 away. How many are left? Now here are 3 beans. Can you take 8 away?
flow.kid: Take 3 beans away from 8. Count what is left. Now try to take 8 away from 3.

ask.q: With adding, the order did not matter. Does the order matter when you take away?
good: Yes. 8 take away 3 works. 3 take away 8 does not.
You cannot take 8 when there are only 3.

flow.parent: 8 take away 3 leaves 5. Nobody can take 8 beans from 3, because the plate is empty after 3. Let your child find this out by trying. Later they will meet numbers below zero, but beans cannot show those.

check.q: 7 beans are on a plate. You take 2 away. How many are left?
check.why: 5. Taking away makes fewer, so the answer must be less than 7. Count back two from 7: 6, 5. Picking 9 means the 2 were added, not taken away.

flow.context: This is step 4 of the Two Plates Test. You take 3 beans from 8, and then you try to take 8 beans from 3.

flow.do: 1. Put 5 beans on your child's plate and 5 on yours. 2. Ask how many you will have together after your child gives you 2. Write the guess. 3. Your child gives you 2 beans. 4. Count each plate, and then both plates together.
flow.say: You have 5 and I have 5. Give me 2 of yours. Together, will we have more, fewer or the same? Why?
flow.kid: You have 5 beans. Give 2 to your grown-up. Count your plate, their plate, and both together.

ask.q: For you, was that adding or taking away? And for me?
good: Taking away for me. I have fewer now.
Adding for you. You got 2 more.
It is both.

flow.parent: Your child now has 3 and you have 7. Together it is still 10. Many children expect the total to change, because something was taken away.
flow.context: This is step 5 of the Two Plates Test. You give 2 of your beans to your grown-up and count both plates.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask your child what they think now, what they saw, and why. 3. Write their words under the table.
flow.say: Look at our table. When did the order matter? When did it not matter? What happened to the beans you gave me?
flow.kid: Look at your table. When did the order matter? When did the number stay the same?

ask.q: What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it is so?
good: Putting together gives the same number both ways.
It was 8 both times, and 16 both times.
Because they are the same beans, only tipped in a different order.
Taking away does not work both ways.
The beans I gave you were not lost. You had them.

check.q: 6 beans and 4 beans make 10. How many do 4 beans and 6 beans make?
check.why: 10. They are the same two heaps, put together in the other order. No bean was added or lost. Picking 'more' or 'fewer' often means the bigger heap going last looked different. Tip the beans both ways to check.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Two Plates Test. You say what you found about order, and about beans that are given away.

activities.title: Five What? One name for both heaps
activities.context: In this activity you add two different kinds of things, such as spoons and tumblers. The point is to see that before you add, you must choose one name that fits both kinds.
activities.problem: 3 spoons and 2 tumblers are 5. But 5 what?

materials.item: other things from around the house, in twos and threes

schedule.what: Add spoons and tumblers, then other pairs of things, and find a name for each total.

activities.record: Write three sums with names, such as '4 chappals + 2 shoes = 6 footwear'. A grown-up can write while the child says them.

setup.art: Three steel spoons and two steel tumblers set out in two groups on a kitchen floor.
setup.caption: 1. Put out 3 spoons and 2 tumblers.

setup.art: A child pushing the spoons and tumblers into one group, with a thought bubble showing the number 5 and a question mark.
setup.caption: 2. Put them together. 5 what?

setup.art: A child carrying two bananas and three oranges in her arms toward the same spot on the floor.
setup.caption: 3. Find two more kinds of things and do it again.

flow.do: 1. Put 3 spoons and 2 steel tumblers on the floor. 2. Ask how many spoons there are, and how many tumblers. 3. Ask how many there are altogether. When your child answers, ask '5 what?'
flow.say: Here are 3 spoons and 2 tumblers. How many are there altogether? Five what?
flow.kid: Put 3 spoons and 2 tumblers together. How many are there? Five what?

ask.q: They are not 5 spoons, and not 5 tumblers. What name fits all five?
good: 5 things.
5 vessels.
5 kitchen things.

flow.context: This is the first step of Five What? You put spoons and tumblers together and look for one name that fits them all.

flow.do: 1. Your child collects two kinds of things from around the house, fewer than 10 of each. 2. They count each kind and add them. 3. They say the total, with a name that fits both kinds. 4. Do this three times and write each sum.
flow.say: Bring me two kinds of things. Add them up. Then tell me the total, and what it is a total of.
flow.kid: Find two kinds of things. Count each kind. Add them. Say a name that fits them all.
flow.parent: Good pairs are chappals and shoes (footwear), bananas and oranges (fruits), pencils and crayons (things to draw with), red beans and white beans (beans). The name is the interesting part, so let your child invent it.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Five What? You add two kinds of things from around the house and give the total a name.

flow.do: 1. Point at one of the mixed heaps. 2. Ask 'How many spoons?' and then 'How many things?' 3. Ask how one heap can have two right answers.
flow.say: How many spoons are here? And how many things? Both answers are right. How can that be?
flow.kid: Look at your heap. How many spoons? How many things? Why are there two answers?

ask.q: Could you add 3 spoons and 2 songs?
good: No. You cannot put them together.
Only if I call them 5 things I like.

check.q: 4 mangoes and 3 bananas are in a bowl. Which is true?
check.why: 7 fruits. 'Fruits' is a name that fits both the mangoes and the bananas. There are still only 4 mangoes and only 3 bananas.

flow.context: This is the last step of Five What? You look at one mixed heap and see that the count depends on the name you choose.

activities.title: Beans, Picture, Sum: show one story three ways
activities.context: In this activity you hear a short story, show it with beans, draw it as dots and write it as a sum. The point is to learn what the signs +, − and = say.
activities.problem: A sum is a very short story. Can you turn a story into a sum, and a sum back into a story?
activities.safety: Keep beans and seeds away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Show an adding story and a taking-away story with beans, dots and a sum. Then make up a story for a sum.

activities.record: Keep the page. Each story is on it twice: as dots and as a sum.

setup.art: Four beans in a row on a sheet of paper with three more beans being placed beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Show the story with beans.

setup.art: The same sheet with four dots and three dots drawn in pencil under the beans.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one dot for each bean.

setup.art: The sheet with 4 + 3 = 7 written under the dots in a child's handwriting.
setup.caption: 3. Write the sum and read it aloud.

flow.do: 1. Tell a short adding story about your home, with numbers up to 10. 2. Your child shows it with beans. 3. Your child draws it as dots. 4. Write the sum together and read it aloud.
flow.say: Listen. 4 crows sat on the wall. 3 more crows came. Show me with beans. Now we write it: 4 + 3 = 7.
flow.kid: Listen to the story. Show it with beans. Draw the dots. Then write the sum.
flow.parent: Say the signs aloud as you write them: 'four plus three equals seven'. The sign = says that both sides are the same amount.
flow.context: This is the first step of Beans, Picture, Sum. You show an adding story with beans, with dots and with a sum.

flow.do: 1. Tell a taking-away story, with numbers up to 10. 2. Your child shows it with beans and takes some away. 3. Your child draws the dots and crosses out the ones taken. 4. Write the sum together: 9 − 2 = 7.
flow.say: 9 murukkus were in the tin. You ate 2. Show me with beans. Now we write it: 9 − 2 = 7.
flow.kid: Show the story with beans. Take some away. Draw the dots and cross some out. Write the sum.
flow.parent: In a taking-away sum, the number you start with is written first. Then comes what is taken, and after the = sign, what is left.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Beans, Picture, Sum. You show a taking-away story with beans, with dots and with a sum.

flow.do: 1. Write a sum with no answer, such as 6 + 5 or 12 − 3. 2. Your child makes up a story for it. 3. Your child finds the answer with beans and writes it. 4. Swap: your child writes a sum for you.
flow.say: Here is a sum: 12 − 3. Make up a story for it. Then find the answer with your beans.
flow.kid: Read the sum. Make up a story for it. Find the answer with your beans.

check.q: 6 children were playing. 2 went home. Which sum fits this story?
check.why: 6 − 2 = 4. Children went away, so it is taking away, and 4 are left. Picking 6 + 2 means the two numbers were put together, but nobody joined the game.

flow.context: This is the last step of Beans, Picture, Sum. You start from a sum and make up a story that fits it.

activities.title: Maths in the kitchen: the vegetable basket
activities.context: In this activity you count the vegetables at home before cooking, and work out how many are left after cooking. The point is to use adding and taking away for a real job in the kitchen.
activities.problem: The cook needs to know two things. How many vegetables do we have? And how many will be left after today's cooking?

materials.item: two kinds of vegetables that are counted one by one, such as tomatoes and onions

schedule.what: Count and add two kinds of vegetables before cooking. Work out what will be left, and check after cooking.

activities.record: Write the day's sums on a slip and stick it on the fridge, for example '5 tomatoes + 4 onions = 9 vegetables' and '5 − 2 = 3 tomatoes left'.

setup.art: A cane basket with five tomatoes and four onions on a kitchen counter, a child sorting them into two groups.
setup.caption: 1. Sort the vegetables into two kinds and count each kind.

setup.art: A child handing two tomatoes and one onion to a mother standing at a stove.
setup.caption: 2. Hand over what the cook asks for.

setup.art: The basket with three tomatoes and three onions left, and a slip of paper with sums stuck on a fridge door.
setup.caption: 3. Work out what is left. Then count to check.

flow.do: 1. Put the tomatoes and the onions in the basket. 2. Your child sorts them into two groups and counts each group. 3. Ask how many vegetables there are in all. 4. Write the sum, with the names.
flow.say: How many tomatoes are there? How many onions? So how many vegetables do we have in all?
flow.kid: Sort the vegetables into two kinds. Count each kind. Add them. How many vegetables in all?
flow.parent: If there are 5 tomatoes and 4 onions, the sum is 5 + 4 = 9 vegetables. The total is 9 vegetables, not 9 tomatoes.
flow.context: This is the first step of the vegetable basket. You count two kinds of vegetables and add them.

chart.title: An example. Your numbers will be your own.

flow.do: 1. Say what today's cooking needs, such as 2 tomatoes and 1 onion. 2. Before your child touches anything, ask how many of each will be left. 3. Your child hands them to you. 4. Your child counts what is left, to check. A grown-up does the cutting and cooking.
flow.say: For the rasam I need 2 tomatoes and 1 onion. How many tomatoes will be left? How many onions?
flow.kid: Listen to what the cook needs. Say how many will be left. Hand them over. Count to check.

ask.q: How did you work it out before counting?
good: I counted back two from 5: 4, 3.
I took them away in my head.

flow.context: This is step 2 of the vegetable basket. You work out how many vegetables will be left after the cook takes some.

flow.do: 1. Ask how many vegetables are left in all. 2. Your child adds the tomatoes left and the onions left. 3. Write the sums on a slip and stick it on the fridge. 4. Ask what must be bought if tomorrow's cooking needs 6 tomatoes.
flow.say: How many vegetables are left in all? Tomorrow I need 6 tomatoes. Do we have enough?
flow.kid: Add what is left. Write the sums. Do you have enough tomatoes for tomorrow?

check.q: There were 6 tomatoes. 2 went into the rasam. How many tomatoes are left?
check.why: 4. The tomatoes that went into the rasam were taken away. Count back two from 6: 5, 4. Picking 8 means the 2 were added. Picking 2 is the number used, not the number left.

flow.context: This is the last step of the vegetable basket. You add what is left, and see whether there is enough for tomorrow.

chart.title: An example: what is left in the basket

activities.title: Maths in a game: sow the seeds as in Pallanguzhi
activities.context: Pallanguzhi is an old board game from Tamil Nadu. It is played with tamarind seeds or cowrie shells on a board with 14 cups. In this activity you borrow its main move, called sowing, on a small board of 6 cups. The point is to watch one cup lose seeds while other cups gain them.
activities.problem: When seeds move from cup to cup, which numbers change, and which number does not?

materials.item: small cups or katoris, or 6 hollows of an egg tray, or 6 circles drawn on paper

activities.safety: Keep beans and seeds away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Set up 6 cups with 3 seeds each. Sow seeds round the board several times. Then count the whole board.

activities.record: Draw the six cups. Write how many seeds are in each at the end. Add them up.

setup.art: Six small steel katoris in two rows of three on a floor, each holding three tamarind seeds.
setup.caption: 1. Six cups in two rows. Put 3 seeds in each.

setup.art: A child's hand lifting all three seeds out of the bottom-left cup, leaving it empty.
setup.caption: 2. Lift all the seeds from one cup.

setup.art: The hand dropping one seed into each of the next three cups, with a curved arrow going round the board.
setup.caption: 3. Drop one seed in each next cup, going round.

flow.do: 1. Set out 6 cups in 2 rows of 3. 2. Your child puts 3 seeds in each cup. 3. Count all the seeds together and write the number.
flow.say: Put 3 seeds in every cup. How many seeds are on the whole board?
flow.kid: Put 3 seeds in each cup. Count all the seeds on the board.
flow.parent: There are 18 seeds. Counting in threes is fine, and so is counting one by one.
flow.context: This is the first step of sowing seeds as in Pallanguzhi, an old Tamil board game. You set up a small board of 6 cups.

chart.title: The small board at the start

flow.do: 1. Your child lifts all the seeds from one cup. 2. They drop one seed in each next cup, going round the board. 3. Ask how many are in the cup they emptied, and in a cup that got a seed. 4. Do this four or five times, from a different cup each time.
flow.say: Pick up all the seeds from one cup. Drop one in each next cup, going round. Which cup has fewer now? Which cups have more?
flow.kid: Lift all the seeds from one cup. Drop one in each next cup. Which cups changed?

ask.q: The cup had 3 and you took 3. How many are in it now? The next cup had 3 and got 1. How many now?
good: None. Zero.

flow.parent: 'Going round' means along your row to the right, and then back along the far row. After a first move from the left cup of your row, the board looks like the picture.
flow.context: This is step 2 of sowing seeds as in Pallanguzhi, an old Tamil board game. You move seeds from one cup into the next cups.

chart.title: After one move from your left cup

flow.do: 1. Ask how many seeds are on the whole board now, after all that moving. Write the guess. 2. Your child counts every cup. 3. Ask why the number is what it is.
flow.say: We moved seeds many times. How many are on the whole board now? More, fewer or the same as at the start? Why?
flow.kid: Guess how many seeds are on the board now. Then count every cup.

ask.q: Seeds were taken away from cups again and again. Why is the total still 18?
good: They only moved to other cups.
What one cup lost, other cups got.
No seed left the board.

flow.parent: The real game has more rules, such as capturing seeds, and families play it in different ways. If a grandparent knows the game, ask them to teach their way.

check.q: A cup has 5 seeds. You lift all 5 and drop them one by one into the next cups. How many are left in that cup?
check.why: 0. You lifted all 5, and 5 take away 5 leaves none. The 5 seeds are not lost. They are in the next five cups, one in each.

flow.context: This is the last step of sowing seeds as in Pallanguzhi, an old Tamil board game. You count the whole board after many moves.

activities.title: When 1 and 1 Make 1: drops and dough
activities.context: In this activity you push two drops of water together, then two balls of dough, then two beans. The point is to see that adding numbers fits things that stay separate, and does not fit things that join.
activities.problem: 1 and 1 make 2. Always? Try it with drops of water.

materials.item: a little water in a tumbler

schedule.what: Push together two drops, then two balls of dough, then two beans. Count each time.

activities.record: Draw three pictures: the drops, the dough and the beans, before and after. Under each, write how many there were and how many there are.

setup.art: A dry steel plate with two round drops of water side by side and a child's wet fingertip above them.
setup.caption: 1. Make 2 drops of water on a dry plate.

setup.art: The same plate with one bigger drop where the two drops were.
setup.caption: 2. Push them together. How many drops now?

setup.art: Two small balls of dough and two beans on the floor beside the plate.
setup.caption: 3. Try it with 2 balls of dough, and then with 2 beans.

flow.do: 1. Dip a fingertip in water and put one drop on a dry steel plate. 2. Put another drop next to it. 3. Ask how many drops there will be if they are pushed together, and why. 4. Your child pushes them together with a finger.
flow.say: Here is 1 drop, and here is 1 drop. If we push them together, how many drops will there be? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Make 2 drops of water on the plate. Guess what will happen. Push them together. How many drops now?
flow.parent: On a dry steel plate the drops stay round. If the plate is wet or soapy the drops spread out, so dry it first.
flow.context: This is the first step of When 1 and 1 Make 1. You push two drops of water together and count the drops.

flow.do: 1. Roll two small balls of chapati dough or clay. 2. Ask how many balls there will be if they are pressed together. 3. Your child presses them into one and rolls it.
flow.say: Here are 2 balls of dough. Press them together and roll. How many balls now? Is the ball the same size as before?
flow.kid: Roll 2 balls of dough. Press them together. How many balls now? Is the ball bigger?
flow.context: This is step 2 of When 1 and 1 Make 1. You press two balls of dough together and count the balls.

flow.do: 1. Put 1 bean next to 1 bean and push them together. 2. Ask how many beans there are. 3. Ask why beans make 2 when drops made 1.
flow.say: Push 1 bean against 1 bean. How many beans? Why do beans make 2, when the drops made 1?
flow.kid: Push 2 beans together. How many beans? Why are beans different from drops?

good: The drops joined, so we cannot count them the same way.
The big drop still has the water of two drops.
Adding works for things that stay separate.

flow.think: What else joins into one when you put two together?

check.q: You push 2 heaps of rice together. What do you get?
check.why: 1 bigger heap. The heaps joined, so the number of heaps went down. No rice was lost: the big heap has all the rice of both. Adding numbers fits things that stay separate, like beans.

flow.context: This is the last step of When 1 and 1 Make 1. You push two beans together and compare them with the drops.

activities.title: Everyone does maths: the chick test
activities.context: In 2009 scientists in Italy tested whether chicks about three days old could follow balls being hidden and moved behind two screens. In this activity you take the chick's place. Beans are hidden under two tumblers and moved across, and you say which tumbler hides more.
activities.problem: A chick could tell which screen hid more balls, without seeing them. Can you?

materials.item: steel tumblers that you cannot see through

activities.safety: Keep beans and seeds away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on them.

schedule.what: Hide beans under two tumblers, move some across, and work out how many are under each.

activities.record: Write the two sums for one round, such as 4 − 2 = 2 and 1 + 2 = 3.

setup.art: Two upturned steel tumblers on a floor, a hand sliding four beans under one, with one bean waiting by the other.
setup.caption: 1. Hide 4 beans under one tumbler and 1 under the other.

setup.art: A hand sliding one bean along the floor from the first tumbler to the second, with a second bean following.
setup.caption: 2. Move 2 beans across, one at a time.

setup.art: A child pointing at the second tumbler with a confident face, both tumblers still down.
setup.caption: 3. Say how many are under each. Then lift.

flow.do: 1. Turn two tumblers upside down. 2. While your child watches, slide 4 beans under one and 1 under the other. 3. Ask which tumbler hides more. Lift both to check.
flow.say: Watch. 4 beans go under this tumbler, and 1 goes under that one. Which tumbler hides more?
flow.kid: Watch the beans go under the tumblers. Point to the one with more. Lift to check.
flow.context: This is the first step of the chick test. Beans are hidden under two tumblers and you say which hides more.

flow.do: 1. Hide 4 and 1 again. 2. Move 2 beans from the tumbler with 4 to the tumbler with 1, one at a time, in plain view. 3. Ask how many are under each now, and which has more. 4. Lift both to check.
flow.say: Now watch. I move 1 bean across. And 1 more. Do not lift! How many are under each tumbler now?
flow.kid: Watch 2 beans move across. Work out how many are under each tumbler. Then lift.

ask.q: How did you know without looking?
good: 4 take away 2 is 2.
1 and 2 more is 3.
I counted back, and then I counted on.

flow.parent: This is one of the moves the chicks watched: 4 and 1 became 2 and 3. About three times in four, the chicks walked to the side with 3. Your child is doing two sums at once: 4 − 2 and 1 + 2.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the chick test. Two beans move from one tumbler to the other, and you work out the new numbers.

rows: 2 beans move from A to B

flow.do: 1. Swap places. Your child hides up to 10 beans under the two tumblers and moves some across. 2. You say how many are under each. 3. Your child lifts the tumblers and checks you.
flow.say: Now you are the scientist and I am the chick. Hide the beans and move some. I will work it out.
flow.kid: Now you hide the beans. Move some across. Check your grown-up's answer.

check.q: 5 beans are under tumbler A and none under tumbler B. You move 3 from A to B. Which has more now?
check.why: Tumbler B. A has 5 take away 3, which is 2. B has none and 3 more, which is 3. Picking A means going by where the beans started, not where they ended.

flow.context: This is the last step of the chick test. You hide and move the beans, and your grown-up works out the numbers.

games.title: Under the Tumbler
games.players: 2 players: with a parent or with a friend. One child alone can play with a dice.
games.context: This is a hiding game with beans and a steel tumbler. Some beans are slid out and the rest stay hidden. You say how many are still hidden, and then lift the tumbler to check. It builds quick taking away.

printables.title: Start cards: how many beans go under the tumbler

rules: Pick a start card, or start with 10. Count out that many beans together and put them under an upside-down tumbler.
The hider tilts the tumbler and slides some beans out, where everyone can see them. The rest stay hidden.
The guesser says how many beans are still under the tumbler, and how they know.
Lift the tumbler and count. If the guesser is right, they win one bean from the spare heap as a point.
Swap jobs after every round. The first player with 5 points wins.
Playing alone: roll a dice and slide out that many beans without looking under the tumbler. Say how many are left, then lift to check. Try to get 5 right in a row.

setup.art: Ten beans being covered by an upturned steel tumbler on a floor, with two children watching.
setup.caption: 1. Count 10 beans. Hide them all under the tumbler.

setup.art: A hand tilting the tumbler and sliding three beans out into view.
setup.caption: 2. Slide some out. The rest stay hidden.

setup.art: A child saying '7!' and the tumbler lifted to show seven beans.
setup.caption: 3. Say how many are hidden. Lift to check.

flow.do: 1. Count out 10 beans together. 2. Put them under an upside-down steel tumbler. 3. Put a small heap of spare beans to one side, for points. 4. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: There are 10 beans under this tumbler. I will slide some out. You tell me how many are still hiding.
flow.kid: Count 10 beans. Hide them all under the tumbler.
flow.context: This is the first step of Under the Tumbler, a hiding game with beans. Here you set up the game.

rows.label: under the tumbler at the start

flow.do: 1. Tilt the tumbler and slide out 3 beans. 2. Ask how many are still under it, and how your child knows. 3. Lift the tumbler and count together.
flow.say: I have slid out 3. There were 10. How many are still under the tumbler? How do you know?
flow.kid: Look at the beans that came out. Say how many are still hidden. Lift to check.
flow.parent: Counting back from 10 is the usual way: 9, 8, 7. Some children count the beans they can see on their fingers and look at how many fingers are still up. Both ways work.

check.q: 10 beans were under the tumbler. 3 are slid out. How many are still under it?
check.why: 7. Three beans were taken away from 10. Count back three: 9, 8, 7. Picking 13 means the 3 were added. Picking 3 is the number you can see, not the number hidden.

flow.context: This is step 2 of Under the Tumbler, a hiding game with beans. Here you play one practice round.

flow.do: 1. Play the game, swapping jobs after every round. 2. Each time, the guesser says how they know. 3. After a few rounds, try a bigger start card.
flow.say: Your turn to hide. Slide some out. I will say how many are left, and you check me.
flow.kid: Play the game. Take turns to hide and to guess. Say how you know.

ask.q: All the beans were slid out. How many are hidden?
good: None.
Zero.

flow.context: This is step 3 of Under the Tumbler, a hiding game with beans. Here you play, taking turns to hide and to guess.

flow.do: 1. Stop when someone has 5 points. 2. Ask which round was the hardest, and why.
flow.say: Who has 5 points? Which round was the hardest to work out?
flow.kid: The first to 5 points wins. Which round was the hardest?
flow.context: This is the last step of Under the Tumbler, a hiding game with beans. Here you finish the game.

games.title: Bigger Total Wins
games.players: 2 or 3 players: with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a card game. Each player turns over two number cards and adds them, and the bigger total wins the round. It builds quick adding, first up to 10 and then up to 20.

printables.title: Number cards from 1 to 10 with dots. Make four of each, or use playing cards from Ace to 10.

rules: For the first game, use only the cards from 1 to 5. Shuffle them and deal them all out, face down. Put aside any cards left over.
Everyone turns over their top two cards and adds them. Say it aloud: '4 plus 3 equals 7.'
The player with the biggest total takes all the cards from that round and puts them in a winnings pile.
If two totals are the same, those players turn over two more cards each. The bigger total takes everything.
When the cards run out, the player with the most cards in their winnings pile wins.
Harder game: use all the cards from 1 to 10. Now the totals go up to 20. Count the dots, or use beans, whenever you need to.
With playing cards, the Ace is 1. Take out the Jacks, Queens and Kings.

setup.art: Two children sitting face to face on a mat, each with a small face-down pile of number cards.
setup.caption: 1. Deal out the cards, face down.

setup.art: One child's two cards turned up, a 4 and a 3 with dots, and the child saying '4 plus 3 equals 7'.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over two cards. Add them and say the total.

setup.art: The child with the total 9 sweeping all four cards into her winnings pile.
setup.caption: 3. The bigger total takes the cards.

flow.do: 1. Make the number cards, or take the Ace to 10 from a pack of playing cards. 2. Keep only the cards from 1 to 5 for now. 3. Shuffle and deal them all out, face down. 4. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: We each turn over two cards and add them. The bigger total wins the cards.
flow.kid: Deal out the cards face down. Do not look at them yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bigger Total Wins, a card game where you add two cards. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: 1. Play one round with the cards face up, slowly. 2. Each player says their total aloud. 3. Ask who has more, and how they know.
flow.say: I turned over 2 and 5. I start at 5 and count on two: 6, 7. What is your total?
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. Add them. Say your total aloud.
flow.parent: Starting from the bigger card is quicker, and it gives the same total. Let your child notice this. If they count all the dots from 1, that is fine.

check.q: You turn over 5 and 4. Your friend turns over 6 and 2. Who has the bigger total?
check.why: You do. 5 + 4 = 9 and 6 + 2 = 8, and 9 is bigger than 8. Picking your friend usually means looking only at the biggest card, the 6. The total uses both cards.

flow.context: This is step 2 of Bigger Total Wins, a card game where you add two cards. Here you play one slow practice round.

flow.do: 1. Play until the cards run out. 2. Now and then, ask which card your child started counting from. 3. If there is time, play the harder game with all the cards.
flow.say: You turned over 2 and 5. Which number did you start counting from? Why?
flow.kid: Play the game. Say each total aloud. The bigger total takes the cards.

good: Yes. Both are 7.
Yes, so I start from 5 because it is quicker.

flow.context: This is step 3 of Bigger Total Wins, a card game where you add two cards. Here you play the game.

flow.do: 1. When the cards run out, each player counts their winnings pile. 2. Ask who has more cards, and how many more.
flow.say: Count your pile. Who won more cards?
flow.kid: Count your pile of cards. Who has more?
flow.context: This is the last step of Bigger Total Wins, a card game where you add two cards. Here you count the cards you won.

games.title: Heads Add, Tails Take Away
games.players: 1 to 3 players: alone, with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a game on a number track from 0 to 20, with a coin and a dice. Heads means hop forward and tails means hop back. It builds counting on and counting back on a number line.

printables.title: A number track of 21 squares, from 0 to 20, to cut out or to draw with chalk

rules: Lay the track in a line from 0 to 20. Each player puts a button on 10.
On your turn, toss a coin and roll a dice.
Heads means add: you will hop forward as many squares as the dice shows. Tails means take away: you will hop back that many.
Before you move, say the sum aloud, such as '10 plus 4' or '10 minus 4', and say where you will land. Then hop, counting each square, to check.
If the hop would take you past 20 or below 0, stay where you are for that turn.
The first player to land on a star square, from 15 to 20, wins.
Playing alone: count how many turns you need to reach a star square. Play again and see whether you need fewer.

setup.art: A chalk number track from 0 to 20 drawn on a floor with stars on squares 15 to 20, and two buttons on square 10.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the track. Put your buttons on 10.

setup.art: A coin showing heads beside a dice showing 4, and a button hopping forward from 10 to 14.
setup.caption: 2. Heads: hop forward by the dice number.

setup.art: A coin showing tails beside a dice showing 3, and a button hopping back from 14 to 11.
setup.caption: 3. Tails: hop back by the dice number.

flow.do: 1. Cut out or draw the 21 squares and lay them in a line from 0 to 20. 2. Mark stars on 15 to 20. 3. Each player puts a button on 10. 4. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: Everyone starts on 10. Heads means hop forward. Tails means hop back.
flow.kid: Lay the track from 0 to 20. Put your button on 10.
flow.context: This is the first step of Heads Add, Tails Take Away, a game on a number track from 0 to 20. Here you set up the track.

flow.do: 1. Play one practice turn each. 2. Show how to say the sum first, then say where you will land, then hop. 3. If you are on 10 with tails and 4, say '10 minus 4 is 6', then hop 9, 8, 7, 6.
flow.say: I am on 10. I got tails and a 4. So it is 10 minus 4. I will land on 6. Now I hop to check.
flow.kid: Toss the coin and roll the dice. Say the sum. Say where you will land. Then hop.
flow.parent: The most common slip is to count the square you are standing on as the first hop. The first hop always lands on the next square.

check.q: You are on 10. You toss tails and roll 4. Where do you land?
check.why: 6. Tails means take away, so you hop back four from 10: 9, 8, 7, 6. Picking 14 means hopping forward, which is for heads.

flow.context: This is step 2 of Heads Add, Tails Take Away, a game on a number track from 0 to 20. Here you practise one turn.

chart.title: You are on 10. Tails and a 4.

flow.do: 1. Play the game. 2. Each player says the sum and the landing square before hopping. 3. Now and then, ask what toss and roll a player is hoping for.
flow.say: You are on 12. What would you like to toss and roll now? Why?
flow.kid: Play the game. Say your sum before you hop. Land on a star to win.

ask.q: You are on 12. What do you need to reach a star?
good: Heads and 3 or more.
12 plus 3 is 15.

flow.context: This is step 3 of Heads Add, Tails Take Away, a game on a number track from 0 to 20. Here you play the game.

flow.do: 1. The game ends when someone lands on a star square. 2. Ask each player where they finished, and how far they were from 15.
flow.say: Who landed on a star first? How far from 15 did everyone else finish?
flow.kid: The first to land on a star wins. Where did you finish?
flow.context: This is the last step of Heads Add, Tails Take Away, a game on a number track from 0 to 20. Here you finish the game.

projects.title: The Banana Diary: five days of adding and taking away
projects.context: In this five-day project you keep a diary for one food at home that is counted one by one, such as bananas, eggs or biscuits. Each morning you count. Each evening you work out how many should be left, and then you check. The point is to use sums to keep track of something real.
projects.problem: How many bananas should be left this evening? Work it out first. Then go and look.

materials.item: a food that is counted one by one: a bunch of bananas, a tray of eggs or a packet of biscuits
a sheet of paper for the diary, with a row for each day

schedule.what: Count the bananas in the morning and write the number. In the evening, ask how many were eaten, work out how many should be left, and then count to check.
Do the same. Write the day's change as a sum, such as 9 − 2 = 7.
If someone buys more, write an adding sum. If not, write a taking-away sum.
In the morning, guess how many will be left by evening. Check in the evening.
Look at all five days. On which day did the number change most? Did it ever go up?

projects.record: A diary with four columns: the day, the number in the morning, what changed, and the number in the evening. Write each day's change as a sum.

example_chart.title: What a diary can look like (your numbers will be your own)

setup.art: A bunch of twelve bananas on a kitchen table beside a sheet of paper ruled into four columns.
setup.caption: 1. Morning: count and write the number.

setup.art: A child at the table in the evening with her back to the bananas, working out a sum on her fingers.
setup.caption: 2. Evening: ask what changed. Work out how many should be left.

setup.art: The child counting the bananas left on the bunch and ticking the diary.
setup.caption: 3. Count to check. Write the sum.

flow.do: 1. Each morning, your child counts the bananas and writes the number in the diary. 2. Ask how many they think will be left by evening.
flow.say: How many bananas are there this morning? Write it down. How many do you think will be left tonight?
flow.kid: Count the bananas. Write the number in your diary.
flow.context: This is the morning step of the Banana Diary, a five-day project. You count the bananas and write the number.

chart.title: An example. Your number will be your own.

flow.do: 1. Each evening, ask the family how many were eaten, and whether any were bought. 2. Before looking, your child works out how many should be left. 3. Your child counts to check, and writes the sum.
flow.say: 3 bananas were eaten today. There were 12 this morning. How many should be left? Now go and count.
flow.kid: Ask how many were eaten. Work out how many should be left. Then count to check.
flow.parent: If the count does not match, that is the interesting part. Did someone eat one without saying? Was one missed in the morning? Let your child find out.

check.q: There were 9 bananas this morning. 2 were eaten. Nobody bought any. How many should be left?
check.why: 7. Eating takes away. Count back two from 9: 8, 7. Picking 11 means the 2 were added.

flow.context: This is the evening step of the Banana Diary, a five-day project. You work out how many bananas should be left, and then count.

chart.title: An example. Your numbers will be your own.

flow.do: 1. On day 5, look at the whole diary together. 2. Ask on which day the number went down most, and whether it ever went up. 3. Ask what made it go up.
flow.say: Look at all five days. When did the number go down most? Did it ever go up? What made it go up?
flow.kid: Look at your diary. When did the number go down most? Did it ever go up?

ask.q: The bananas that were eaten were taken away from the bunch. Where did they go?
good: Into us.
Into our tummies.
They became part of the family.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Banana Diary, a five-day project. You look back over five days of sums.

challenges.title: Stretch: pay 8 when you have only 5
challenges.context: This is a design challenge that goes past Class 1. In a shop game you must pay more than you have. You invent a way to write down what you still owe, so that nobody forgets.
challenges.problem: You are playing shop. You have 5 beans as money. A toy costs 8 beans. The shopkeeper lets you take it today and pay the rest later. Invent a way to show exactly how much you still owe.
constraints: Anyone who looks at your record must be able to tell how much you owe.
When you pay some of the debt later, your record must show the debt getting smaller.
You may use beans of two colours, paper, a pencil and cups.
materials: 10 beans of one colour, such as rajma
10 beans or seeds of another colour, such as white chana or groundnuts
general: Draw 3 empty circles for the beans you still have to give. Fill one in each time you pay a bean.
creative: Use a second colour of bean for what you owe. In old China, people used red sticks for what they had and black sticks for what they owed.
Draw a number line that goes on to the left of zero, and put a mark three hops to the left.
Write the number you owe with a dot over it. Many old Indian maths books marked a debt that way.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Then test it. You earn 2 beans, and then 4 more. Show on your record what you owe after each.

setup.art: A child handing five beans to a parent playing shopkeeper, with a small toy on the floor between them and a slip of paper marked 8.
setup.caption: 1. The toy costs 8 beans. You have 5. Pay what you can.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with three empty circles drawn on it, labelled 'I owe', beside a cup holding three white beans.
setup.caption: 2. Invent a way to show what you still owe.

setup.art: The child filling in two of the three circles after handing over two more beans.
setup.caption: 3. Pay some more. Change your record.

flow.do: 1. Give your child 5 beans. You are the shopkeeper. 2. Say that the toy costs 8 beans, and that they may take it today. 3. Your child pays what they can. 4. Ask how many more they must bring tomorrow.
flow.say: The toy costs 8 beans. You have 5. Pay me what you have. How many do you still owe me?
flow.kid: Pay 5 beans for a toy that costs 8. How many do you still owe?

good: I counted on from 5 to 8: 6, 7, 8.
8 take away 5 is 3.

flow.parent: Counting on from 5 to 8 gives 3. If your child says 'I have none left, so I owe nothing', lay 8 beans in a row and cover 5 of them.
flow.context: This is the first step of the challenge Pay 8 When You Have Only 5. You pay what you can and work out what you still owe.

flow.do: 1. Ask how the debt could be written down so that nobody forgets it. 2. Let your child try an idea of their own. 3. If they want ideas, read the usual ways and the creative ways aloud.
flow.say: Tomorrow we may forget. How can we show that you owe me 3 beans?
flow.kid: Think of a way to show that you owe 3 beans. Make it.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the challenge Pay 8 When You Have Only 5. You invent a way to record a debt of 3 beans.

flow.do: 1. Give your child 2 beans as pay for a small job. 2. They pay you and change their record. 3. Give 4 more. They pay what is still owed and keep the rest.
flow.say: Here are 2 beans for helping me. Pay your debt. What do you owe now? Here are 4 more.
flow.kid: You get 2 beans. Pay them. What do you owe now? Then you get 4 more.
flow.parent: Owing 3 and paying 2 leaves a debt of 1. Then, out of 4 more beans, 1 pays the debt and your child keeps 3.

check.q: You owe 3 beans. You pay 2. How many do you still owe?
check.why: 1. Paying makes a debt smaller: 3 take away 2 is 1. Picking 5 means the 2 were added to the debt.

flow.context: This is step 3 of the challenge Pay 8 When You Have Only 5. You pay off the debt bit by bit and change your record.

flow.do: 1. Draw a number line from −5 to 5, with zero in the middle. 2. Say that people write 'owe 3' as −3, three hops to the left of zero. 3. Ask where 'owe 1' would sit.
flow.say: People write 'owe 3' as minus 3. It sits 3 hops to the left of zero. Where is 'owe 1'?
flow.kid: Find zero on the number line. Hop 3 to the left. That is 'owe 3'.
flow.context: This is the last step of the challenge Pay 8 When You Have Only 5. You see how people write a debt on a number line.

items.p: How many beans in all? 4 + 2 = ____
items.why: There are 4 beans, and 2 more are coming. Count on from 4: 5, 6.

items.p: How many dosas are left? 7 − 3 = ____
items.why: Take 3 away from 7. Count back three: 6, 5, 4. So 4 dosas are left.

items.p: 5 idlis are on the plate. 3 more come. Which sum fits?
items.why: More idlis came, so the two groups are put together. That is adding: 5 + 3 = 8.

items.p: 3 + 6 and 6 + 3 give the same total.
items.why: True. Both are 9. The same two groups are put together, only in a different order.

items.p: Work out this sum. 8 + 2 = ____
items.why: Start at 8 and count on two: 9, 10.

items.p: 9 crows sit on a wire. 2 fly away. How many are left?
items.why: Flying away is taking away. Count back two from 9: 8, 7. Picking 11 means the 2 were added.

items.p: Match each sum to its answer.
items.why: 2 + 3 = 5. 6 − 2 = 4. 4 + 4 = 8. 7 − 1 = 6. Use beans to check each one.
True. Adding zero means adding nothing, so the 6 stays 6.

items.p: Start on 12. Hop forward 3. Where do you land? ____
Draw 5 laddus. Then draw 2 more. Write the sum under your picture.
items.a: 7 laddus in all, and the sum 5 + 2 = 7.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the two groups. The sum says that they were put together.

items.p: Draw 8 balloons. Cross out 3 that popped. Write the sum.
items.a: 8 balloons with 3 crossed out, and the sum 8 − 3 = 5.
items.why: Crossing out shows taking away. 5 balloons are not crossed out.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. Why do 3 and 5 make the same total as 5 and 3?
items.a: Because they are the same beans. Only the order changed, and no bean was added or lost.
items.why: A strong answer says that the total depends on which beans are there, not on which heap went first.

items.p: Start on 9. Hop forward 4. 9 + 4 = ____
items.why: From 9, hop forward four: 10, 11, 12, 13.

items.p: Work out this sum. 15 − 3 = ____
items.why: Count back three from 15: 14, 13, 12.

items.p: A full ten-frame and 6 more beans. 10 + 6 = ____
items.why: Ten and six more is sixteen. Count on from 10 if you need to: 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16.

items.p: Which is the quickest right way to work out 2 + 9?
opts: Start at 2 and count on nine
Start at 9 and count on two
items.why: You can add in either order, so start with the bigger number. From 9, count on two: 10, 11. Starting at 2 also gives 11, but it takes nine hops.
Taking away all 13 leaves none. None is zero.

items.p: You take 4 beans away from 11 beans. Now there are more than 11 beans.
items.why: False. Taking away makes fewer. 11 − 4 = 7, and 7 is less than 11.

items.p: Put these sums in order, from the smallest answer to the biggest.
Sort each story: is it adding or taking away?
items.why: When something joins the group, it is adding. When something leaves the group, it is taking away.

items.p: Draw a number line from 0 to 20. Show 14 − 5 with hops. Write the answer.
items.a: Five hops back from 14, landing on 9.
items.why: The hops back land on 13, 12, 11, 10, 9. So 14 − 5 = 9.

items.p: Make up a story for the sum 12 − 4. Say it aloud. A grown-up writes it.
items.a: Any story where 12 things are there and 4 leave, so that 8 are left. For example: 12 eggs were in the tray, 4 were used, and 8 are left.
items.why: A strong story has something going away, and ends with 8.

items.p: Meena gives 2 of her 5 murukkus to her brother Arun, who has 1.

views.says: That was taking away. I had 5 and now I have 3.
That was adding. I had 1 and now I have 3.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that both are right. It was one move: 5 − 2 = 3 for Meena and 1 + 2 = 3 for Arun. Together they still have 6.
items.why: Whether a move is adding or taking away depends on whose murukkus you are counting. The number the two have together did not change.

items.p: Draw 3 idlis and 2 vadas on a plate. Then finish the sentence: There are 5 ____.
items.a: A plate with 3 idlis and 2 vadas, and a name that fits both, such as 'things to eat' or 'snacks'.
items.why: They are not 5 idlis, and not 5 vadas. The total needs a name that fits both.

items.p: 8 beans, and 5 more. 8 + 5 = ____
items.why: Two of the five fill the ten. Three are left over. Ten and three is 13.

items.p: Start on 17. Hop back 8. 17 − 8 = ____
This goes past Class 1. Three heaps: 4 + 3 + 2 = ____
items.why: Put the first two together: 4 + 3 = 7. Then add the last: 7 + 2 = 9. Any order gives 9.

items.p: There were 9 beans. Some are hidden now. You can see 6. How many are hidden?
items.why: Count on from 6 to 9: 7, 8, 9. That is 3. Picking 15 means the two numbers were added.

items.p: Which of these cannot be done with beans?
items.why: With 4 beans on the plate, you cannot take 9 away. The other two can be done: 9 − 4 = 5 and 4 + 9 = 13.

items.p: 7 + 6 = 13. Without counting, what is 6 + 7?
items.why: 13. Adding in the other order gives the same total.

items.p: Adding always makes a number bigger.
items.why: False. Adding zero leaves the number the same: 8 + 0 = 8. Adding one or more does make it bigger.

items.p: 2 drops of water pushed together make 2 drops.
items.why: False. They join into one bigger drop. Adding numbers fits things that stay separate, like beans.

items.p: Match each sum to the story that fits it.
pairs: 6 crows on a wire, 3 more land
6 idlis on a plate, 3 are eaten
9 seeds in a cup, 6 are lifted out
items.why: Stories where things join are adding. Stories where things leave are taking away. The first number in a taking-away sum is how many there were at the start.

items.p: 5 − 5 = 0, but 5 − 0 = 5. Why are the answers different? Say it aloud.
items.a: In the first sum all five are taken away, so none are left. In the second sum none are taken away, so all five are left.
items.why: A strong answer says what the zero means in each sum: none left, or none taken.

items.p: This goes past Class 1. Draw a number line from −3 to 3. Circle the place for 'I owe 2'.
items.a: A line with −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3 on it, and a circle on −2.
items.why: Owing 2 is written −2. It sits two hops to the left of zero.

items.p: One drop of water is pushed into another drop. Now there is one drop.

views.says: 1 + 1 is always 2. Drops are just the wrong thing to count.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other girl has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason. For example: the numbers 1 and 1 always make 2, but the sum only fits things that stay separate.
items.why: Mathematicians say that 1 + 1 = 2 is always true for numbers. Whether it fits what is in front of you depends on what you count.

quiz.p: Look at the picture. How many beans in all? 6 + 3 = ____
quiz.why: There are 6 beans, and 3 more are coming. Count on from 6: 7, 8, 9.

quiz.p: A full ten-frame has 10 beans. 5 more are beside it. How many beans?
quiz.why: Ten and five more is fifteen. Picking 105 means writing the two numbers side by side. Adding puts the beans together.

quiz.p: 8 bananas are in a bunch. 2 are eaten. How many are left?
quiz.why: Eating takes away. Count back two from 8: 7, 6. Picking 10 means the 2 were added.
14 is ten and four. Take the four away, and ten is left.

quiz.p: Which sum says '7 take away 2 leaves 5'?
quiz.why: The sign − means take away. The number you start with comes first, then what is taken, then = and what is left.

quiz.p: The sign = means that both sides are the same amount.
quiz.why: True. In 4 + 2 = 6, the 4 + 2 on one side and the 6 on the other side are the same amount.

quiz.p: You are on 11 on the number line. You hop forward 4. Where do you land?
quiz.why: From 11, hop 12, 13, 14, 15. Picking 14 means the 11 was counted as the first hop. Picking 7 means hopping back.

quiz.p: How do you work out 16 − 3 on a number line?
quiz.why: Taking away is hopping back. Start on 16 and hop 15, 14, 13. The answer is 13.
13. Adding in the other order gives the same total, because the same two groups are put together.

quiz.p: With beans, you can do 9 − 4, and you can also do 4 − 9.
quiz.why: False. You can take 4 beans from 9. You cannot take 9 beans from 4, because the plate is empty after 4. In taking away, the order matters.
Adding zero means adding nothing, so 7 stays 7. Picking 0 mixes this up with taking everything away.

quiz.p: 9 laddus are on a plate. All 9 are eaten. How many are left?
quiz.why: Taking away all of them leaves none. None is zero: 9 − 9 = 0.

quiz.p: You have 6 beans and Amma has 4. You give Amma 2. How many do you two have together now?
quiz.why: 10, the same as before. The 2 beans only moved from your plate to Amma's. Now you have 4 and she has 6.

open_questions.q: Is 1 + 1 = 2 true everywhere in the universe, or only where there are separate things to count?

maths.problem: In Bigger Total Wins you turn over 3 and 9. Your friend turns over 6 and 5. Who wins the round?
maths.answer: You do. Your total is 12 and your friend's total is 11.
maths.explain: For 3 + 9, start at the bigger number, 9, and count on three: 10, 11, 12. For 6 + 5, start at 6 and count on five: 7, 8, 9, 10, 11. 12 is one more than 11, so you win.
maths.context: In the card game Bigger Total Wins, each player turns over two cards and adds them. The bigger total wins.
maths.why_maths: Adding gives each player's total. Comparing the two totals tells you who wins.

maths.problem: On the small Pallanguzhi board the six cups hold 0, 4, 4, 4, 3 and 3 seeds. How many seeds are on the whole board? Could you have known without adding?
maths.answer: 18 seeds. Yes: the board started with 18, and no seed has gone from the board.
maths.explain: Add the cups: 0 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 3 + 3 = 18. But there is a quicker way. Sowing only moves seeds from cup to cup. What one cup loses, other cups gain. So the total is still the 18 you started with.
maths.context: When you sowed seeds as in Pallanguzhi, you lifted the seeds from one cup and dropped one in each next cup.
maths.why_maths: Knowing what does not change saves you from adding six numbers.

maths.problem: On Monday morning there were 12 bananas. 3 were eaten on Monday and 4 were eaten on Tuesday. How many are left on Wednesday morning?
maths.explain: After Monday: 12 − 3 = 9. After Tuesday: 9 − 4 = 5. So 5 bananas are left.
maths.context: In the Banana Diary you counted in the morning and worked out how many should be left in the evening. Here are two days in a row.
maths.why_maths: Taking away twice tells you what is left without going to look.

maths.problem: You tip 6 beans and 5 beans together and count 12. Then you tip 5 beans and 6 beans together and count 11. Can both counts be right? What should you do?
maths.answer: No. The total must be the same both ways. Count again, sliding each bean. It is 11.
maths.explain: The same beans are on the plate both times, so the number cannot change. One of the counts went wrong: a bean got two numbers. Count on from 6 to check: 7, 8, 9, 10, 11. So 6 + 5 = 11 and 5 + 6 = 11.
maths.context: In the Two Plates Test you put two heaps together in both orders and got the same total each time.
maths.why_maths: Knowing that the order cannot change the total lets you catch a counting slip.

maths.problem: In Under the Tumbler there are 10 beans. Slide 1 out and 9 are hidden. Slide 2 out and 8 are hidden. What happens to the hidden number each time one more bean comes out? How many are hidden when 6 are out?
maths.answer: The hidden number goes down by 1 each time. When 6 are out, 4 are hidden.
maths.explain: Each bean that comes out is one fewer under the tumbler. 10 − 6 = 4. The beans outside and the beans hidden always make 10 together.
maths.context: In the game Under the Tumbler, some of 10 beans are slid out and you say how many are still hidden.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern lets you say the hidden number at once, without counting back each time.

maths.problem: This one is harder. You have 8 beans and Amma has 2. How many must you give her so that you both have the same number?
maths.explain: Together you have 10 beans, and giving does not change that. For both to have the same, each needs 5. You go from 8 down to 5 by giving 3. Amma goes from 2 up to 5 by getting 3.
maths.context: In the Two Plates Test you gave 2 of your beans to your grown-up. Your plate went down, their plate went up, and the total stayed the same.
maths.why_maths: One move changes two heaps at once. Taking away and adding together tell you what a fair share needs.

warmup.q: You have 7 beans and give away 2. How many do you have now?

roots.context: We put beans together, took beans away and passed them from plate to plate. Now let us think about what taking away really is.

deep_truth.truth: Take 2 beans from your plate and give them to Amma. For you it is taking away. For Amma it is adding. It is one move with two names. Count both plates together, and no bean is lost.
deep_truth.habit: We think 'taken away' means gone. But the beans only moved. Whether we call the move adding or taking away depends on whose plate we look at.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Two Plates Test you gave away 2 of your 5 beans. Your plate went down to 3, the other plate went up to 7, and together there were still 10.

three.who_am_i: You are giving and getting all day. The idli taken from your plate is added to you. The breath that leaves you is added to the air in the room.
three.what_is_life: Other living beings keep track of more and fewer too. A chick three days old can follow balls as they are added and taken away behind a screen.
three.what_is_this_world: In the world, things mostly move. Rain is taken from the cloud and added to the river. We choose where to look, and then we call it adding or taking away.

roots.thread: Start with nothing. Add one bean, and you have one. Keep adding one, and you can reach any number. Take them away one by one, and you are back at nothing. And when beans only move from plate to plate, the number of beans in all stays as it was.

teachings.teaching: The verse says: that is whole, and this is whole. Take the whole from the whole, and the whole is still there.
teachings.link: With beans, taking away leaves fewer on the plate. But count every plate together and nothing is missing. The verse speaks of a whole like that, which giving does not make smaller.

teachings.teaching: Anaxagoras was a Greek thinker who lived about 2,500 years ago. He said that nothing truly begins or ends. Things are only mixed together and separated again.
teachings.link: That is putting together and taking apart. He thought every change in the world was one of these two.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka tells his son that if you know one lump of clay, you know everything made of clay. The pot and the plate differ only in name.
teachings.link: To add idlis and vadas, you look past their two names and find one name that fits both.

science.text: When a puddle dries, the water is not gone. It has moved into the air. Scientists have found that in everyday changes, stuff is never lost. It only moves or changes form. Antoine Lavoisier showed this in France more than 200 years ago, by weighing things before and after they burned. Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier worked with him in the laboratory and drew the instruments.

Chicks three days old, honeybees and human babies five months old have all followed small numbers of things being added and taken away in tests. Scientists still argue about what goes on in their minds as they do it.

other_view.view: They say a sum talks about one heap only. 8 − 2 = 6 is true whether the 2 beans went to Amma, rolled under the fridge or were eaten. And some things really do end. A popped balloon is not a balloon anywhere else. So taking away is real, they say, and not only a way of looking.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people come to write adding and taking away the way we do? This card tells the true story of the signs +, − and =, and of an argument that lasted hundreds of years.
how_we_found_out.story: People have added and taken away for as long as they have shared and traded, long before anyone wrote sums. For most of that time, sums were written in words. In the year 628 the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta wrote rules for adding and taking away, in Sanskrit verse. His rules covered zero, and also debts, which are numbers below zero. An old Indian book, the Bakhshali manuscript, used a small cross after a number to mean 'take this away'. In Europe the signs + and − were first printed in 1489, in a German book for merchants by Johannes Widmann. The sign = came in 1557, from Robert Recorde, a Welsh doctor. For hundreds of years many European mathematicians said that you could never take a bigger number from a smaller one. In 1544 Michael Stifel called such answers 'absurd numbers'. But the rules for debts gave right answers every time people used them, for money and later for cold temperatures. Slowly everyone came to accept numbers below zero.
how_we_found_out.who: Brahmagupta, Johannes Widmann, Robert Recorde and many others
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: You can never take a bigger number from a smaller one. With beans that is true. But Brahmagupta's rules for debts, written in 628, showed how to do it with numbers, and they give right answers for money owed and for temperatures below zero.

The Bakhshali manuscript: a cross like + written after a number marks it as negative or to be subtracted (G. R. Kaye's 1927 edition; MacTutor; Bodleian Library). Its date is debated, so the unit says only 'more than a thousand years ago'.

Johannes Widmann, Behende und hubsche Rechenung auff allen Kauffmanschafft (Leipzig, 1489): first printed + and − signs. Robert Recorde, The Whetstone of Witte (1557): the = sign. Michael Stifel, Arithmetica integra (1544): 'numeri absurdi'.
Liu Hui's commentary on the Nine Chapters (263 CE): red counting rods for positive numbers and black for negative. A dot over a number for a negative in many Indian texts (noted by Kaye).
Primary teeth: 20 in all, 10 upper and 10 lower; shedding usually starts at about age 6 (standard dental references).
Hindu lunar calendar: 15 tithis in the waxing half (shukla paksha) and 15 in the waning half (krishna paksha).

Pallanguzhi: a two-player sowing game on a board of 2 rows of 7 cups, played with tamarind seeds or cowries, sown counter-clockwise; the number of seeds and the capture rules vary by family and region.
Antoine Lavoisier, Traité élémentaire de chimie (1789), with plates engraved by Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier: careful weighing before and after burning (conservation of mass).
Anaxagoras, fragment DK 59 B17, as given in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Anaxagoras.
Number-selective nerve cells: Nieder, A., Freedman, D. J. and Miller, E. K. (2002), Science 297, 1708-1711 (monkeys); Ditz, H. M. and Nieder, A. (2015), PNAS 112, 7827-7832 (crows).

playtest: Walked through every flow as a family of two in a flat. The Two Plates Test needs 20 beans and three plates, and the counts come out the same in both orders unless a bean rolls away, so work on plates. Under the Tumbler, Bigger Total Wins and Heads Add, Tails Take Away were played through in the head. Bigger Total Wins with the cards 1 to 5 lasts five rounds for two players. Heads Add, Tails Take Away usually ends in about eight turns each, and a player can never be stuck. The sowing activity was checked move by move: after one move from the left cup the cups hold 0, 4, 4, 4, 3 and 3, and the total stays 18. The drops stay round only on a dry steel plate. Step minutes add up to each activity's minutes.
